title: generics constraints and generic methods
concepts: A generic type or method is written once with type parameters and works with caller-supplied type arguments. The compiler substitutes those arguments for type checking while preserving static type safety; this is not the same as storing every value as object and casting later.

Constraints state what a type argument must support. They let a generic implementation safely use capabilities such as construction, reference identity, value semantics, a base class, an interface, or a static operator contract.

Generic inference often lets callers omit type arguments, but inference has defined inputs and does not infer from a desired return type. Constraints validate inferred candidates; they do not generally make inference discover a type argument by searching all possible types.

Generic types and methods participate in overload resolution. Variance, constraints, nullable annotations, and runtime representation each have distinct rules; changing one does not imply a change in the others.

Choose a generic abstraction when the same algorithm or data shape has meaningful behavior across multiple types. Avoid a type parameter that is used only once without expressing a relationship, and prefer the narrowest constraint that captures the required capability.

versionNotes.edition: C# 13 and current C# 15 generic constraint behavior
items: C# 13 added the `allows ref struct` anti-constraint, permitting ref struct type arguments when the generic declaration follows ref-safety rules. C# 15 adds closed hierarchies and union types; their syntax and exhaustiveness behavior are treated in the dedicated type-shape and pattern-matching topics.
